title: Adapter pattern
idea: The Adapter pattern lets your code call a class with the wrong interface by wrapping it in a class that implements the interface you expect.

analogy.text: A travel plug adapter: your charger keeps its plug, the wall keeps its socket, and a small piece in between makes them fit.
analogy.breaks: A plug adapter passes power through; a code adapter converts data too.

points: The adapter implements your target interface and wraps the foreign class, the adaptee.
The adapter only translates names, units, codes, results and errors; it adds no features.
`InputStreamReader` adapts a byte `InputStream` into a character `Reader`; `Arrays.asList` adapts an array.
Skip it when you own both sides: change the interface instead of wrapping it.

messages.label: quotePence(Parcel GB, 2500 g)
messages.note: Checkout holds a `RateProvider`. It has never heard of FastShip.

messages.label: getRate(2.5, "GBR")
messages.note: The adapter maps `GB` to `GBR` and grams to kilograms. Only it ever calls the vendor SDK.

messages.label: "GBP 6.00"
messages.note: The vendor answers with a price as text, in its own format.

messages.label: 600 (long pence)
messages.note: The adapter parses it with `BigDecimal` and returns the type the target promised.

messages.label: quotePence(Parcel US, 500 g)
messages.note: Next, a destination the vendor does not serve.

messages.label: getRate(0.5, "USA")
messages.note: US maps to USA and 500 g becomes 0.5 kg, exactly as before.

messages.label: throws UnsupportedDestinationException
messages.note: The vendor signals failure with a magic string, not an exception.

messages.label: throws UnsupportedDestination
messages.note: The adapter turns the vendor's error into our own exception type.

code.title: The problem: vendor leaks
code.caption: Two services call the vendor SDK directly; each repeats the translation, and each gets it wrong differently.

walk.text: The vendor SDK speaks kilograms, 3-letter country codes and text prices. You cannot change it.
`Checkout` hand-translates codes, units and the price string. Any unknown country is silently priced as Ireland.
`Returns` copied the call but missed steps: grams go in as kilograms, and `IE` is never mapped.
The output: a US parcel quoted as Irish, a huge price, and a raw vendor error string.
Swapping carriers now means editing every class that touches `FastShipClient`.

code.title: The fix: one adapter
code.caption: All translation lives in `FastShipAdapter`; the rest of the code sees only `RateProvider`.

walk.text: The target interface speaks our domain: a `Parcel` in, a price in pence out.
The `Parcel` record validates once, so the adapter never sees a zero-gram parcel.
Object adapter: it implements the target and holds the adaptee by has-a composition, injected through the constructor.
Input translation: country codes via a fixed map, grams to kilograms. An unknown code fails loudly.
Error translation: the vendor's magic string becomes our own unchecked exception.
Output translation: `BigDecimal` parses the text exactly; `longValueExact` throws rather than silently truncate.
The only client line that names FastShip. A new carrier needs one new adapter and this line.

pitfalls: Caching or retries inside the adapter mix jobs; use a decorator (same-interface wrapper, c07-t04) instead.
Letting vendor types such as error strings leak through the target interface defeats the adapter.
Class adapters (`extends` the adaptee) expose every adaptee method; prefer wrapping by composition.

quiz.q: Your code depends on `RateProvider`. A second carrier's SDK offers `price(Shipment)`, and you want every quote logged. Best design?
options: An adapter for the SDK, wrapped in a logging decorator
Make the adapter also log, to keep one class
Subclass the new SDK and override `price` to log
quiz.why: The adapter only converts interfaces. Logging keeps the same interface and adds behaviour, which is a decorator's job. Changing the target bends your code to one vendor.

takeaway: An adapter changes the interface, never the behaviour.
